title: Marfan mouse and human aortic tissue
sample_processing: High-throughput quantitative proteomics were performed by multiplexed isobaric labeling in aortic tissue from 12-week-old C57BL/6 MFS mice and WT littermates as controls. Each TMT 10-plex batch contained biological replicates from each experimental condition and an internal standard for TMT comparison. Peptides were TMT-labeled according to the manufacturer’s instructions and desalted on OASIS extraction cartridges. Labeled peptide samples were analyzed using a Proxeon Easy nano-flow HPLC system (Thermo Fisher Scientific; Waltham, USA) coupled via a nanoelectrospray ion source (Thermo Fisher Scientific) to either a Q-Exactive HF mass spectrometer (Termo Fisher Scientific) or an Orbitrap Fusion mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Proteins were identified by searching against a mouse database (UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot and TrEMBL December_2020) supplemented with 116 CRAP proteins (Global Proteome Machine), totaling 50915 sequences.
description: Thoracic aortic aneurysms and dissections (TAAD), as occur in Marfan syndrome (MFS), currently lack a cure. Our previous studies revealed that overactivation of the AKT-NO signaling pathway mediates aortic disease in MFS. However, the mechanisms upstream of AKT activation remained poorly understood. Here we identify the Fibronectin-αVβ3-PI3K-PIP3-PDK1-ILK cascade as a critical mediator of AKT-NOS2 upregulation and aortic disease in MFS. We show that fibronectin (FN) accumulates in the walls of human and mouse MFS aortas. Disrupting FN multimerization inhibits AKT activation and NOS2 induction in vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs), prevents aortic contractility dysregulation, and reverses aortic dilation in MFS mice. Mechanistically, both human and mouse MFS aortas exhibit αVβ3 and ILK upregulation. Pharmacological inhibition of αVβ3, PI3K, PDK1, and ILK, or their recruitment to the plasma membrane by PIP3, prevents FN-induced AKT activation and NOS2 upregulation in VMSCs and aortic contractility dysregulation. Furthermore, ILK inhibition or aortic silencing reverses aortic disease, while its deletion in smooth muscle cells prevents aortic growth in MFS mice. These findings establish the most thoroughly characterized pathway implicated in MFS to date and suggest a causative role for the FN-αVβ3-PI3K-PIP3-PDK1-ILK-AKT-NOS2 cascade in human TAAD, highlighting its components as potential targets for therapeutic intervention.
data_processing: Quantitative results were expressed as log2(Ai/C), where Ai is the intensity of the TMT reporter for the corresponding sample I, and C is the mean intensity of the TMT reporters from the controls or the mean value of the internal reference standards. Log2(ratios) from reporters were integrated to protein levels and statistical analysis was performed using iSanxot.

title: Generation and Proteomic Analysis of Fibrin-Based 3D Engineered Vascular Tissues (EVTs) from Human Aortic Smooth Muscle Cells
sample_processing: Engineered Vascular Tissue (EVT) was washed with 1.5 mL pre-warmed PBS for 3 x 5 min in a cell culture incubator at 37°C and 5% CO₂. EVT was cut into smaller pieces and incubated with tissue lysis buffer (TLB, 20 mM Tris-HCl, 113 mM NaCl, 5 mM EDTA, 2 mM EGTA, 1% Triton X-100, 0.1% SDS, with protease inhibitors and phosphatase inhibitors, pH 7.4) for 24 hours with vigorous shaking at 1400 rpm to isolate soluble extracellular and intracellular proteins. After transferring the supernatant to a new tube, the pellet was incubated in guanidine hydrochloride buffer (4 M GuHCl, 50 mM sodium acetate, 12.5 mM EDTA, with protease inhibitors and phosphatase inhibitors, pH 5.8) for 48 hours with gentle shaking at 750 rpm to isolate less soluble, highly crosslinked extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins. The TLB and GuHCl fractions (10 µg) were precipitated by adding 10 volumes of ice-cold ethanol and incubated overnight at -20°C. After centrifuging at 18,000 × g for 30 min at 0°C, the ethanol supernatant was discarded and the pellet was dried using vacuum concentrator. The protein samples were deglycosylated in 20 µL deglycosylation buffer (150 mM NaCl, 50 mM sodium acetate, 10 mM EDTA, pH 6.8) containing the following enzymes: Chondroitinase ABC (1:100), Heparanase (1:500), Endo-β-Galactosidase (1:500), β1,4-Galactosidase (1:200), β-N-Acetylglucosaminidase (1:200), α2-3,6,8,9 Neuraminidase (1:200) and Endo-α-N-Acetylgalactosaminidase (1:200). The samples were incubated at 25°C, 200 rpm for 2 hours followed by 37°C, 200 rpm for 24 hours. Afterwards, the samples were dried with a vacuum concentrator, resuspended in 20 µL of H₂¹⁸O with PNGase F (1:100) and incubate at 37°C, 200 rpm for 24 hours. The deglycosylated protein samples were reduced and denatured in 6 M urea, 2 M thiourea, 10 mM dithiothreitol for 1 hour at 37°C, alkylated by addition of 50 mM iodoacetamide and incubated for 1 hour at RT in the dark. The alkylated proteins were precipitated in 10 volumes of ice-cold ethanol overnight. Pellet was dried and resuspended in 0.1 M triethylammonium bicarbonate (TEAB) buffer pH=8.5. Trypsin/Lys-C solution was used for digestion at enzyme: protein ratio = 1:25, and incubate for 18 hours at 37°C, 200 rpm. The digestion was stopped by 1% trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) and peptide cleanup was carried out using C18 cartridges on Bravo AssayMAP robotic system. The eluate was dried and resuspended in 1% acetonitrile (ACN), 0.1% formic acid (FA). Peptide samples were analysed by LC-MS/MS with the following parameters: the Vanquish Neo HPLC was setup using trap and elute configuration with PepMap Neo Trap Cartridge (0.3 mm x 5 mm) and EASY-Spray PepMap RSLC C18 column (2 µm, 15 cm x 150 µm). Mobile phase A is 0.1% FA in H₂O, mobile phase B is 80% ACN, 0.1% FA in H₂O. The elution gradient is: 0 min – 1 min, 2% – 7% B, 5 µL/min; 1 min – 2 min, 5% – 10% B, 5 – 1.25 µl/min; 2 min – 16.5 min, 10% – 35% B, 1.25 µL/min; 16.5 min – 18.5 min, 35% – 45% B, 1.25 µL/min; 18.5 min – 19 min, 45% – 99% B, 1.25 µL/min; 19 min – 20 min, 99% B, 5 µL/min; equilibration using 4x column volumes of mobile phase A. Data independent acquisition (DIA) was used on FAIMS (CV=-48V) coupled to Astral Zoom Mass Spectrometer: Full MS Scan was acquired using Orbitrap with scan range of 380 m/z – 980 m/z and resolution of 240,000; Normalized AGC Target is 500% and Max Injection Time is 3 ms; DIA MS2 spectra were acquired using Astral analyzer covering 380 m/z – 980 m/z with 200 fixed-width isolation windows (3 m/z) without overlapping and with Window Placement Optimization; the HCD Normalized Collision Energy is 25%; Normalized AGC Target is 500% and Max Injection Time is 7 ms.
description: Vascular smooth muscle cells (SMCs) reside within the medial layer of blood vessels, where they interact with an extracellular matrix (ECM) composed of collagen, elastin, and proteoglycans to maintain vascular structure and function. Aberrant ECM remodeling contributes to multiple vascular diseases; however, conventional two-dimensional culture systems do not adequately recapitulate the three-dimensional (3D) cellular and matrix environment required to study smooth muscle cell–ECM interactions and matrix remodeling. This protocol describes the generation of engineered vascular tissues (EVTs) from primary human aortic SMCs cultured within fibrin-based 3D hydrogels. Following casting between flexible polydimethylsiloxane posts, EVTs undergo cellular alignment, contraction, and deposition of de novo ECM, providing a physiologically relevant platform for studying vascular matrix biology. The protocol details tissue fabrication, culture, harvesting, and downstream analysis of newly deposited ECM. In addition, a workflow is presented for qualitative and quantitative characterization of EVT-derived proteins using Western blotting and mass spectrometry-based proteomics. Sequential protein extraction enables assessment of soluble and ECM-enriched protein fractions, facilitating in-depth evaluation of ECM composition. This platform provides a reproducible approach for investigating ECM production and remodeling by human SMCs in a 3D environment.
data_processing: The RAW files were analysed by Spectronaut version 21.0.260609.94842 (Lovell) Enterprise (x64) using directDIA Workflow: Trypsin/P was used as enzyme with 2 missed cleavages allowed; Human 1 gene 1 protein database version 202601 (20,659 entries) and Bovine 1 gene 1 protein database version 202601 (20,666 entries), plus Trypsin and LysC sequences, were used; Carbamidomethyl (C) was set as fixed modification and Acetyl (Protein N-term), Deamidation 18O (N), Oxidation (M), Oxidation (P), Oxidation (K) were used as variable modifications; Experiment Precursor and Protein Qvalue Cutoff was set at 0.01. PG.Quantity was exported for further analysis. Non-human proteins, proteins with PG.Qvalue ≥ 0.01, and proteins without UniProt ID-to-gene name mapping were removed from the dataset. Imputation was performed with the following strategy: for proteins with data completeness > 80% in one group, < 70% overall, and < 50% in the other group, replace missing values with 20% of the protein's minimum observed abundance before log₂ transformation; apply k-nearest neighbour (KNN) imputation (k = 5) after log₂ transformation for remaining proteins with ≥ 70% overall data completeness. Differential protein expression analysis was then performed using the limma package on the log₂-transformed, imputed protein abundance matrix: a paired linear model was fitted, including donor as a blocking factor and extraction group (TLB vs GuHCl) as the experimental variable of interest. Empirical Bayes moderation was applied to improve variance estimation across proteins. Differential expression was assessed by comparing GuHCl relative to TLB, yielding log₂ fold changes, moderated t-statistics, P-values, adjusted P-values (FDR), and 95% confidence intervals.

title: Post-transcriptional glucocorticoid receptor signalling synchronises circadian rhythms
sample_processing: Cell pellets were resuspended in 200µL of lysis bu?er [20mM HEPES containing 0.1% RapiGest (Waters)] with 2µL 250U/µL molecular grade benzonase (Millipore Sigma, E8263) and incubated for 30min at RT. Total protein in each sample was quantified using the Pierce Coomassie Plus (Bradford) Assay Kit (23236) according to the manufacturer?s instructions and normalised to total protein. Samples were incubated with 4mM dithiothreitol (DTT), vortexed and incubated at 60°C for 10min. Iodoacetamide was then added to a final concentration of 14mM and mixed in by vortexing and incubated for additional 45min in the dark, at room temperature. To digest protein into peptides, trypsin was added at a ratio of 50:1 protein: trypsin and samples incubated for 10h at 37°C, shaking at 450RPM. Following digestion, samples were briefly spun down to isolate the digest at the bottom of the tube. To label peptides, TMTPro stock solution was added at a 5:1 ratio of TMT: protein. For the TMT internal bridge channel, a pooled control containing equal protein amount from all samples was prepared. Samples were vortexed for 5s, spun down, then incubated for 1h at RT with gentle vortexing every 5min (2850RPM for 10s). The TMT labelling reaction was quenched by incubation with 5µL of 5% hydroxylamine (0.4% (v/v) final) (ThermoFisher, 90115) for 15min at RT in 500mM HEPES. Labelled samples were then pulled into a single low bind tube. To remove ACN, the multiplexed sample was dried to completion in a vacuum centrifuge. 100µL trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) 0.5% (v/v) was then incubated with the multiplexed sample for at least 45min at 37°C. The sample was then centrifuged at 13,000xg for at least 15min at 4°C to remove all insoluble RapiGest byproducts, and supernatant carefully removed to ensure no particulates remained. Pierce Peptide Desalting Spin Columns (ThermoFisher, 89852) were then used to desalt the sample. To condition the spin columns, the white tip at the bottom of the column was discarded, and the column centrifuged within a 2mL microcentrifuge tube at 2,000xg for 1min to remove the solution and pack the resin material. Columns were then washed 2X with 300µL ACN, then washed 2X with 0.1% TFA in water. The multiplexed sample was then completely dissolved in 200µL of 0.1% TFA in water, before loading onto the column and centrifuging at 3,000xg for 1min. Sample-bound columns were then washed 3X with 300µL 0.1% TFA. To completely remove excess TMT reagent, columns were washed 2X with 300uL 5% methanol, 0.1% TFA solution. Elution of the desalted sample from the column was performed by loading 300µL of 50% ACN, 0.1% TFA solution and centrifuging for 1min 2X. The liquid contents of each sample were evaporated to dryness by vacuum centrifugation using a SpeedVac Concentrator. Multiplexed samples were then fractionated using basic reverse phase into 12 final non-contiguous concatenated fractions per plex. Phosphopeptide enrichment was performed using KingFisher (TiO2 high-transluency (HT)   and ZrO2 HT). 20µL of Ti-IMAC HP beads were added to 200µL of Loading bu?er (1M glycolic   acid in 80% ACN and 5% TFA), and the microsphere washed with 500µL of Loading bu?er.   Dried sample was then resuspended in 200µL of Loading bu?er before adding to beads.   Beads were then washed with 500µL of Loading bu?er, followed by 500µL of Wash bu?er 1   (80% ACN, 1% TFA) then 500µL of Wash bu?er 2 (10% ACN, 0.2% TFA). Samples were eluted   with 200µL of Elution bu?er (1% NH4OH). The above procedure was then repeated using ZrO2 beads.
description: Circadian rhythms are driven by cellular clocks throughout the body that maintain optimal health. Glucocorticoid (GC) hormones are vital for synchronising cellular clocks, aligning them with external day/night cycles, but mechanistic understanding is incomplete. We use a glucocorticoid receptor KO/rescue approach to show residue E755 and N-terminal intrinsically disordered region are essential for GC synchronisation, whereas nuclear translocation from the cytoplasm is not. Using nascent and mature transcriptomics with (phospho)proteomics we show that, under physiological GC increases, the GR regulates a substantial proportion of gene expression post-transcriptionally. Rapid upregulation of Per1 mRNA occurs through increased RNA processing not synthesis, which drives GC synchronisation via acute increases in nascent PER1 and not PER2 protein. We find synchronisation to a single GC dose is highly heterogeneous between individual cells. Our findings provide mechanistic insight into nuclear hormone receptor signalling and establishes a cellular basis for the gradual alignment of circadian clocks by daily environmental cycles via systemic cues.
data_processing: Raw data were imported and data processed in Proteome Discoverer v3.1 (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The raw files were submitted to a database search using Proteome Discoverer with SequestHF against the?Mus musculus. Common contaminant proteins (several types of human keratins, BSA and porcine trypsin) were added to the database. The spectra identification was performed with the following parameters: MS accuracy, 10 p.p.m.; MS/MS accuracy of 0.6 Da for spectra acquired in Ion trap mass analyzer; up to two missed cleavage sites allowed; carbamidomethylation of cysteine and TMTpro 16 plex on lysines?and peptide N-terminal?as a fixed modification; and oxidation of methionine as variable modifications. Percolator node was used for false discovery rate estimation and only rank 1 peptide identifications of high confidence (FDR<1%) were accepted.

title: GDF15 Resolves Liver Inflammation in MASH Independently of Reductions in Food Intake or Weight Loss
sample_processing: Plasma proteomics sample preparation A DDA library was generated using pooled plasma either neat or with Proteominer enrichment (BioRad). For the Proteominer-based preparation, the eluted proteins were precipitated in TCA (20% final) to remove denaturants present in the elution buffer prior to continuing. For the DIA samples, 2.5 μl of neat plasma was used. Proteins were reduced and alkylated in PBS containing 1% sodium deoxycholate (SDC), 10 mM triethylammonium bicarbonate (TEAB) pH 8.5, 5 mM tris(2-carboxyethyl)phosphine (TCEP) and 10 mM chloroacetamide (CAA) by heating for 15 min at 70°C. Upon cooling, a trypsin/LysC protease mix (Promega) was added in an enzyme:protein ratio of 1:50 (w/w) and digestion was performed at 37°C for 16 h. The reaction was quenched by acidification to a final concentration of 1% formic acid (FA) and precipitated SDC was removed by centrifugation. Peptides were purified on SepPak C18 columns (Waters), eluted in two steps (40% ACN followed by 60% ACN in ddH2O) and evaporated to dryness by speedvac centrifugation. Library samples were reconstituted in 5 mM ammonium biocarbonate (ABC) buffer pH 8 for subsequent high-pH fractionation. DIA samples were reconstituted in 0.1% FA for direct LCMS analysis. For each library sample, 40 μg of peptide was fractionated into 20 linear fractions by high-pH reverse-phase chromatography using an Acquity CSH C18 column (1.7 μm × 150 mm) (Waters, Milford, MA, USA) on an Ultimate 3000 HPLC system (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Peptides were loaded onto the column in Buffer A (5 mM ABC pH 8) and eluted at 30 μl/min in a linear gradient from 5% to 25% Buffer B (5 mM ABC pH 8 in 90% ACN) in 35 min, followed by a 5 min increase to 70% B, 5 min at 70% B, 5 min from 70% to 5% B and finally 5 min at 5% B. The fractions were acidified using FA, evaporated by speedvac centrifugation and reconstituted in 0.1% FA prior to LC-MS analysis.   LCMS Measurement of plasma proteomes Samples were measured on an EASY-nLC 1200 ultra-high pressure system (Thermo Fisher Scientific) coupled via a nano-electrospray ion source to a Q Exactive HF-X Orbitrap mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Peptides were separated using a 45 cm PepSep column (100 μm internal diameter, packed with ReproSil C18 1.5 μm resin), maintained at 60°C using a Pharmafluidics μPAC Butterfly column oven, over a 60 min gradient at a flowrate of 300 nl/min. Samples were loaded in Buffer A (0.1% FA) and eluted in 45 min from 10% to 30% Buffer B (0.1% FA in 80% ACN), followed by 5 min from 30% to 45% B, 3 min from 45% to 80% B, 3 min at 80% B, 2 min from 80% to 5% B, and finally 3 min at 5% B.  Spray voltage was set to 2 kV, funnel RF level 40 and heated capillary temperature 275°C. For library generation, 1 μg of peptide from each fraction was analyzed using a TopN data-dependent MS/MS scan method. Full scan spectra were acquired from 375 to 1500 m/z at 60,000 resolution and an automatic gain control (AGC) target of 3 × 106 charges or a maximum injection time of 25 ms. The 10 most abundant peptides were selected with a 1.3 m/z isolation window and a fixed first mass of 100 m/z. Dynamic exclusion was set to 30 s to avoid repeated sequencing of the same peptide. Fragmentation of precursor ions was performed by higher-energy C-trap dissociation with a normalized collision energy of 28 eV. MS2 spectra were recorded at 45,000 resolution with an AGC target of 1 × 105 and a maximum injection time of 86 ms. For DIA experiments, 0.5 μg of peptide was analyzed per sample. The method consisted of a survey scan from 350 to 1400 m/z at 60,000 resolution and an AGC target of 3 × 106 charges or a maximum injection time of 45 ms. Precursor peptides were isolated in 35 variable length windows (2 windows of 30 m/z, 24 windows of 18 m/z, 7 windows of 30 m/z, one window of 100 m/z and one window of 284 m/z) with an overlap of 1 m/z and a fixed first mass of 100 m/z. Fragmentation of precursor ions was performed by higher-energy C-trap dissociation with a normalized collision energy of 25 eV. MS2 spectra were recorded at 30,000 resolution with an AGC target of 3 × 106 and a maximum injection time of 50 ms.
description: Growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF15) is strongly associated with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), yet whether it drives disease or protects against liver injury remains unresolved. Using thermoneutral mouse models that closely mimic human MASH, we show that loss of GDF15 or its receptor GFRAL selectively worsens hepatic inflammation and fibrosis independently of steatosis or insulin resistance. Conversely, recombinant GDF15 suppressed liver inflammation and fibrosis more effectively than matched caloric restriction despite equivalent reductions in food intake, body weight, and steatosis. Spatial transcriptomics and bulk RNA-seq revealed that GDF15 remodels the hepatic immune-fibrotic niche by suppressing pro-inflammatory macrophages, plasma B cells, and activated stellate cells while promoting pro-resolving immune programs. These effects required GFRAL but occurred independently of β-adrenergic signaling. In a steatosis-free CCl₄ model, GDF15 retained potent anti-inflammatory effects and activated hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis and hepatic glucocorticoid receptor (GR) signaling, which were blunted by GR antagonism. Together, these findings identify GDF15 as an endogenous neuroimmune regulator that restrains liver inflammation and fibrosis independently of weight loss or steatosis through a GFRAL–HPA–GR signaling axis.
data_processing: Mass spectrometric data analysis DDA MS data were analyzed using MaxQuant software (version 1.6.7.0)1,2 with the integrated Andromeda algorithm3 and searched against the Mus musculus Uniprot complete proteome reference database using default settings.1,2 A 1% false discovery rate was applied at PSM, protein and peptide level, allowing 2 missed cleavages (Trypsin/P) as well as fixed (cysteine carbamidomethylation) and variable (N-terminal acetylation, methionine oxidation) modifications. Results from the MaxQuant output tables (msms, evidence files) were imported into Spectronaut software (version 15, Biognosys) to generate a spectral library. DIA MS data were analyzed using Spectronaut software (version 15, Biognosys). Default settings were used, with exception of cross-run normalization based on Qvalue sparse and local normalization. The data was quantile normalized using the Bioconductor package in R4 and further processed using Perseus software (version 1.6.15.0).5 The data was filtered for a minimum of five valid values per group and a two-sample t-test with permutation-based statistics (FDR 0.05, S0 0.1) was used to identify significantly regulated proteins. Gene ontology (GO) enrichment analysis was conducted using Fisher’s exact test with multiple testing correction. Principle component analysis (PCA) was performed on proteins filtered for 100% valid values.

title: BioID2-based proximity labeling identifies DDIT4-interacting proteins in human coronary artery smooth muscle cells
sample_processing: Primary human coronary artery smooth muscle cells (HCASMCs) were cultured and transduced with adenoviruses encoding BioID2-NC or BioID2-DDIT4 for 36 hours. Biotin (50 μM, Sigma, B4501) was then added to the culture medium for an additional 16 hours to allow biotinylation of proximal proteins. Cells were harvested and lysed on ice using IP lysis buffer (Beyotime, P0013) supplemented with protease inhibitors (Roche, 04693159001). Lysates were cleared by centrifugation and incubated with streptavidin-coupled magnetic beads (Invitrogen, 65601) to enrich biotinylated proteins. Beads were washed extensively, and bound proteins were eluted using appropriate elution buffer. A fraction of the eluted proteins was subjected to SDS-PAGE and Western blot analysis to confirm biotinylation efficiency. The remaining eluted proteins were separated by gel electrophoresis. Protein bands were excised from the gel and subjected to in-gel tryptic digestion. Extracted peptides were desalted and dried prior to mass spectrometry analysis.
description: DDIT4 (DNA damage-inducible transcript 4) is a stress-responsive protein that has been implicated in vascular smooth muscle cell (VSMC) phenotypic switching and vascular remodeling. However, the comprehensive protein interaction network of DDIT4 in VSMCs remains poorly characterized. In this study, we employed BioID2-based proximity labeling to identify DDIT4-interacting proteins in primary human coronary artery smooth muscle cells (HCASMCs). HCASMCs were transduced with adenoviruses encoding BioID2-NC (negative control) or BioID2-DDIT4 fusion protein for 36 hours, followed by supplementation with 50 μM biotin (Sigma, B4501) for 16 hours to label proximal proteins. Biotinylated proteins were enriched using streptavidin-coupled magnetic beads (Invitrogen, 65601), separated by SDS-PAGE, and subjected to in-gel tryptic digestion. The resulting peptides were analyzed by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) on an Orbitrap Fusion Lumos mass spectrometer. Protein identification was performed by searching the acquired spectra against the UniProt protein database. This dataset provides a resource for understanding the DDIT4 interactome in VSMCs and may offer insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying DDIT4-mediated VSMC phenotypic modulation.
data_processing: Raw data were searched against the UniProt human Swiss-Prot database (20,308 sequences) using Mascot v2.3 (Matrix Science) with the following parameters: trypsin (≤1 missed cleavage); peptide mass tolerance 10 ppm; fragment mass tolerance 0.02 Da; fixed modification: carbamidomethylation (C); variable modifications: oxidation (M), pyro-Glu (N-term Q), deamidation (NQ). Search results were rescored with Percolator and filtered at PSM-level FDR ≤ 1%. Protein inference was performed using the parsimony principle.

title: Quantitative proteomics of mitochondria isolated from rat pulmonary arterial smooth muscle cells under normoxia and chronic hypoxia
sample_processing: Mitochondria were isolated from cultured rat PASMCs after 48 h at 21% or 1% O2 by hypotonic swelling and Teflon homogenisation, followed by differential centrifugation at 800 x g and 10,000 x g. Peptides were generated from the mitochondrial fraction using S-Trap mini columns. Protein concentration was measured with the DC Protein Assay. 100 ug of protein was digested overnight at 37 C with 10 ug trypsin. Peptide concentration was measured with the Pierce Quantitative Peptide Assay.
description: Primary pulmonary arterial smooth muscle cells (PASMCs) were isolated from rat lungs by an arterial tracing method and cultured to passage 4. Cells were exposed to normoxia (21% O2) or hypoxia (1% O2) for 48 h. A mitochondria-enriched fraction was prepared from each culture and analysed by label-free data-independent acquisition on an Orbitrap Astral Zoom. The dataset supports a methods paper describing the isolation technique and was used to confirm induction of cytochrome c oxidase subunit 4 isoform 2 (COX4I2) at the protein level. Three biological replicates per condition.
data_processing: Peptides were separated on an Evosep Eno system with an IonOpticks Aurora Elite XT column (75 um x 15 cm) using the 40 samples-per-day Whisper Zoom method and analysed on a Thermo Orbitrap Astral Zoom in data-independent acquisition mode. MS1 spectra were acquired in the Orbitrap at 240,000 resolution over 380-980 m/z; MS2 spectra were acquired in the Astral analyser using HCD at 25 percent normalised collision energy with 300 sequential 2 m/z isolation windows. Raw files were processed in Spectronaut and searched against the UniProt Rattus norvegicus reference proteome (UP000002494). Protein groups quantified in all runs were retained. Intensities were expressed as a fraction of the summed intensity of all mitochondrial proteins in each run and log2-transformed. Differential abundance between hypoxia and normoxia was assessed by unpaired two-tailed Student t-test assuming equal variance, with Benjamini-Hochberg correction reported as the false discovery rate.

title: The smooth muscle titin filament system  regulates uterus contractility and implantation.
sample_processing:
Peptide identification by mass spectrometry. After protein separation using polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (PAGE), titin bands were cut and gel pieces were subjected to tryptic in-gel digestion followed by stage-tip peptide desalting. Samples were measured by LC‐MS/MS on a Q Exactive Plus mass spectrometer (Thermo) connected to an EASY-nLC system (Thermo).
Spatial Proteomics Sample Preparation. Laser microdissected samples were lysed, reduced and alkylated in 2 µl lysis buffer (0.1% DDM, 5 mM TCEP, 20 mM CAA in 100 mM TEAB pH 8.5 in water). Plates were closed with a PCR ComfortLid (Hamilton) and incubated for 1h at 95°C in a thermal cycler. Samples were cooled down and proteins were sequentially digested. First, 1 µl Lys-C (prediluted in water to 2 ng/µl) was added and digested for at least 2h at 37°C in a thermal cycler (lid temperature: 50°C). Following, 1 µl trypsin (prediluted in water to 2 ng/µl) was added and incubated in the thermal cycler at 37°C overnight. The reaction was quenched with 1 µl TFA (1 % final concentration) and vacuum dried (20 min at 60°C) before peptide-cleanup. 	
Peptide cleanup with C18-tips. Peptide cleanup was performed with Evotips (EV2011, Evosep, Odense, Denmark) as recommended by the manufacturer with all centrifugation steps being performed for 1 min at 800 g. Briefly, Evotips were rinsed with 20 ul Solvent B (0.1 % FA in ACN). The tips were conditioned by soaking in Isopropanol for approx. 10 sec. and equilibrated by adding 20 µl Solvent A (0.1% FA in LC-MS grade water). The peptide samples in the 384 well plate were resuspended in Buffer A, loaded to the Evotip and once washed. Cleaned Peptides were eluted with 20 µl Buffer into a 96-well plate and vacuum dried (15 min at 60°C). The plate was stored at -20°C until LC-MS measurement. Before analysis, 4.2 µl of MS loading buffer (3% ACN, 0.1% FA in LC-MS water) were added, briefly vortexed and centrifuged. The plate was closed with a silicon mat, 4 µl sample were injected for MS analysis. 
Liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (LC – MS) analysis.  For LC-MS analysis, a setup of an EASYnLC-1200 system (Thermo Fisher Scientific) connected to a trapped ion mobility spectrometry quadruple time-of-flight mass spectrometer (timsTOF Ultra2, Bruker Daltonik) with a nano-electrospray ion source (CaptiveSpray, Bruker Daltonik). The autosampler was configured to pick samples from 96-well plates. Peptides were seperated on a 20-cm home-packed HPLC column (75-mm inner diameter packed with 1.9-mm ReproSil-Pur C18-AQ silica beads, Dr. Maisch), using a linear 44 minute gradient at a flow rate 250 nl/min. The gradient consisted of an increase from 5% to 30% buffer B over 29 mins, followed by a ramp to 60 % buffer B over 3 mins. This was succeeded by a 5 minutes wash at 90%  buffer B and a final re-equilibrating step of 5 mins at 50% buffer B. The total gradient length was 44 minutes. Column temperature was kept consistent at 40 °C using a column oven. For dia-PASEF analysis, we used a dia-PASEF method with 8 dia-PASEF scans separated into 3 ion mobility windows per scan covering a 400-1000 m/z range by 25 Th windows and an ion mobility range from 0.64 to 1.37 Vs cm-2. The mass spectrometer was operated in high sensitivity mode, with an accumulation and ramp time at 100 ms, capillary voltage set to 1750V and the collision energy as a linear ramp from 20 eV at 1/K0 = 0.6 Vs cm-2 to 59 eV at 1/K0 = 1.6 Vs cm-2. The collision energy was ramped linearly as a function of ion mobility from 59 eV at 1/K0 = 1.6 V s cm-2 to 20 eV at 1/K0 = 0.6 V s cm-2.
description: Titin is a giant protein of vertebrate striated muscles where it determines sarcomere structure and elastic properties. Its role in smooth muscle is poorly understood, but preliminary data suggests the presence of a truncated titin isoform that interacts with α-actinin and myosin. Here we demonstrated that full length titin exists in the myometrium of the uterus, where it forms a discrete filament system. In smooth muscle specific knockout mice deficient in titin’s C-terminal kinase region, myometrial morphology was normal but oxytocin-induced contractility was increased. Animals were fertile, but titin deficient uteri displayed fewer implantation sites, mislocalization, and crowding with increased placental weights. The phenotype relates to elevated expression of p62 and calmodulin, which bind titins kinase region and affect uterine proteostasis and smooth muscle tone. This study provides evidence for titin’s role in mechanotransduction with potential clinical relevance towards optimizing implantation after in vitro fertilization and ectopic pregnancy.
data_processing:
Gel-based experiment. Database search was performed with MaxQuant version 1.6.10.43, adding Oxidation (M) and N-terminal acetylation as variable modifications. An FDR of 0.01 was applied for peptides and proteins and the Andromeda search was performed using a mouse Uniprot database using the match-between-runs feature. Decoy hits and contaminants were filtered out from the resulting peptides table.
Spatial Proteomics raw data analysis. Proteomics raw files were processed using DIA-NN (version 2.0 Academia) with a predicted mouse library (mouse2023_contaminant. predicted.speclib). DIA-NN was operated in the default mode with minor adjustments. Briefly, MS1 and MS2 accuracies were set to 15.0 and MBR enabled. Missed cleavages were set to 2 maximum number variable modifications to one with N-terminal M excision, C carbamidomethylation and oxidation(M) selected.

title: Optimizing efficacy to safety ratio of glucocorticoids in rheumatoid arthritis models by leveraging PPARα agonism
sample_processing: Preparation of LC-MS/MS samples.   OA-FLS cells were seeded in three technical replicates in 12-well plates (100,000 cells/well) and, 24h later, were serum deprived for 16h prior to compound stimulations. FLS cells were washed with ice-cold PBS, collected with 5% SDS / 50 mM triethylammonium bicarbonate (TEAB), snap-frozen and stored at -80 °C until further processing. The lysate was transferred to a 96-well PIXUL plate and sonicated with a PIXUL Multisample sonicator (Active Motif) for 5 minutes with default settings (Pulse 50 cycles, PRF 1 kHz, Burst Rate 20 Hz). Next, samples were centrifuged for 15 minutes at 2,204 xg at RT to remove insoluble components. Proteins were reduced and alkylated by addition of 10 mM Tris(2-carboxyethyl)phosphine hydrochloride and 40 mM chloroacetamide and incubation for 10 minutes at 95°C in the dark. Phosphoric acid was added to a final concentration of 2.75% and subsequently samples were diluted 7-fold with binding buffer containing 90% methanol in 100 mM TEAB, pH 7.55 (binding buffer). After loading the samples to S-trap micro columns (Protifi) using centrifugation for 1 min at 1,500 xg, the columns were washed 3 times with 150 µl binding buffer using the same centrifugation settings. Digestion of the proteins was done by addition of 20 µl 50mM TEAB containing 1 µg of trypsin and incubation overnight at 37°C. Peptides were eluted in 3 times, first with 40 µl 50 mM TEAB, then with 40 µl 0.2% formic acid (FA) in water and finally with 40 µl 0.2% FA in water/acetonitrile (ACN) (50/50, v/v). Eluted peptides were dried completely by vacuum centrifugation. The dried peptides were redissolved in 20 µl 0.1% trifluoroacetic acid in water/acetonitrile (98/2, v/v), diluted 100-fold with 0.1% formic acid (FA) of which 20 µl was loaded on Evotips (Evosep, P/N EV2011, Odense, Denmark) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. All loaded Evotips were stored in 0.1% FA at 4°C until LC-MS/MS analysis could be started. LC-MS/MS analysis.  FLS cells were washed with ice-cold PBS, collected with 5% SDS / 50 mM triethylammonium bicarbonate (TEAB), snap-frozen and stored at -80 °C until further processing. Samples were run in data-independent parallel accumulation serial fragmentation (DIA-PASEF) mode on an Evosep One LC-system (Evosep) in-line connected to a timsTOF SCP (Bruker, Belgium). Peptides were analyzed with the 20 SPD whisper method using the Aurora Gen3 Elite column (15cm x 75 µm I.D., 1.7µm beads, Evosep), heated to 50°C. Peptides were eluted from the column through the predefined 20SPD whisper gradient consisting of 0.1% FA in LC-MS-grade water as solvent A and 0.1% FA in ACN as solvent B. Eluting peptides were measured in positive polarity with a full-scan range of 100 m/z to 1700 m/z. The trapped ion mobility spectrometry (TIMS) was operated at a fixed duty cycle close to 100%, a ramp and accumulation time of 100 ms, ranging from 1/K0 =0.64 Vscm2 to 1/K0 =1.50 Vscm2. Collision energy was linearly ramped as a function of the inverse mobility from 20 eV at 1/K0=0.60Vscm2 to 59 eV at 1/K0 = 1.60 Vscm2. A DIA-PASEF mass range of 400 Da to 1000 Da was used in a mobility range of 1/K0 =0.64 Vscm2 to 1/K0 =1.37 Vscm2 using a window size of 25 Da according to supplementary table S1, resulting in a cycle time of 0.96s.
description: Glucocorticoids remain essential therapies for immune- and inflammatory diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis (RA) but are notorious for their metabolic side effects. Given the anti-inflammatory and metabolically favorable actions of peroxisome-proliferator activated nuclear receptor (PPAR) agonists, we investigated whether PPARα agonism could enhance the therapeutic efficacy and/or mitigate the metabolic side effects of glucocorticoids.
data_processing: LC-MS/MS data analysis.  LC-MS/MS runs of all samples were searched together using the DiaNN algorithm (version 1.8.1). Spectra were searched against the human protein sequences in the Swiss-Prot database (database release version of 2023_08), containing 20,423 sequences. Enzyme specificity was set as C-terminal to arginine and lysine, also allowing cleavage at proline bonds with a maximum of 2 missed cleavages. Variable modifications were set to oxidation of methionine residues and acetylation of protein N-termini. Fixed modification was set to carbamidomethylation of cysteine residues. Default settings were mainly used, except for the addition of a 400-1000 m/z precursor mass range filter and MS1 and MS2 mass tolerance was set to 15 and 20 ppm, respectively. Further data analysis of the shotgun results was performed with an in-house script in the R programming language (version 4.2.2). Protein expression matrices were prepared as follows: the DIA-NN main report output table was filtered at a precursor and protein library q-value cut-off of 1% and only proteins identified by at least one proteotypic peptide were retained. After pivoting into a wide format, iBAQ intensity columns were then added to the matrix using the DIAgui’s R package get_IBAQ function (26). Groups of 7,650 proteins were reliably quantified using protein group maximum likelihood quantification (PG.MaxLFQ), with at least 3 valid values in one of the experimental conditions.  Proteomics data were log2-normalized and missing protein intensity values were imputed by randomly sampling from a normal distribution centered around each sample’s noise level (package DEP) (27). Principle component analysis was performed using R. To compare protein abundance between pairs of sample groups, statistical testing for differences between 2 group means was performed, using the package limma (28), with a false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.05, log fold change of ≥ 2- or ≤ 0.5-fold (|log2FC| ≥ 1) and adjusted p-value < 0.05. Ingenuity pathway analysis (IPA) was performed for gene set enrichment analysis and network analysis on all proteins with an FDR and adjusted p-value < 0.05, without applying an additional log-fold change threshold (|log₂FC| ≥ 1). Heatmap visualization, and hierarchical clustering was exclusively applied on all interferon-stimulated genes-proteins present in the dataset, using hierarchical clustering of z-scored log2 PG.MaxLFQ intensities (metric: one minus pearson correlation; linkage method: average; cluster: columns).
